subject: Cooking
title: Joël Robuchon: The Chef of the Century
description: A micro-lesson that makes Joël Robuchon: The Chef of the Century usable.

hook.text: Joël Robuchon earned 32 Michelin stars — more than any chef who ever lived. His secret weapon? Mashed potatoes.

buildup.text: Robuchon's purée de pommes uses equal parts potato and butter — a 1:1 ratio that horrified nutritionists.

discovery.text: Named 'Chef of the Century' by the Gault-Millau guide in 1990, his precision was legendary.

twist.text: He retired at 51, then un-retired to create L'Atelier — casual counter-service fine dining, defying his own legacy.

climax.text: L'Atelier proved that Michelin-star quality could exist without white tablecloths and formality.

punchline.text: The world's greatest chef proved luxury could feel casual.

quiz.question: What was Joël Robuchon's famous signature dish?
options: Mashed potatoes with a 1:1 potato-to-butter ratio

details.summary: Joël Robuchon held more Michelin stars than any chef in history — 32 at his peak. Named Chef of the Century by the Gault Millau guide, he was known for obsessive perfection in classical technique. His mashed potatoes, using equal parts butter, became the most famous side dish in fine dining.
details.whyItMatters: Robuchon proved that classical technique executed at the highest level remains relevant alongside avant-garde innovation. His L'Atelier concept also democratized fine dining through open counter seating.
takeaways: He held 32 Michelin stars simultaneously at his peak — a world record
His mashed potatoes use a 2:1 potato-to-butter ratio by weight
L'Atelier replaced formal dining rooms with open kitchen counter seating

faq.question: What made Robuchon's technique exceptional?
faq.answer: His obsession with precision was legendary. He weighed ingredients to the gram, timed cooking to the second, and expected identical results every service. His mashed potatoes required passing through a sieve three times.

faq.question: How did L'Atelier change fine dining format?
faq.answer: L'Atelier replaced white tablecloths and formal service with counter seating facing an open kitchen. The atmosphere was relaxed yet the food was three-star quality. Portions were smaller, prices lower, and seating casual. This format made Robuchon's cooking accessible to a wider audience globally.
